mechanism: Habsburg Spain under Philip II became the main military patron of the Catholic Counter-Reformation, enforcing Tridentine reform across its territories.
Spain's Habsburg monarchy financed and armed its Austrian cousins, drawing Madrid into the Thirty Years' War after 1618.
Philip II's centralization, Catholic repression and heavy taxation in the Netherlands provoked the Dutch Revolt against Spanish rule.
British colonial expansion after the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi brought land seizures that triggered the New Zealand Wars against Maori iwi.
Muhammad's preaching and revelations in Mecca and Medina founded Islam, establishing its scripture, community and law.
Muhammad's revelations, recited and compiled after his death, formed the Quran, Islam's central scripture.
After Muhammad's death, the Muslim community's caliphs built the Rashidun Caliphate, extending Islamic rule across Arabia and the Levant.
Umayyad-led Muslim armies crossed into Iberia in 711 and conquered the Visigothic kingdom, establishing Al-Andalus.
The Abbasid revolution overthrew the Umayyads in 750 and founded an Islamic caliphate centred on Baghdad, claiming religious legitimacy.
Japanese occupation during World War II weakened French colonial control of Indochina, enabling Cambodian demands for independence.
Jesus's teaching and crucifixion gave rise to the early Christian movement, which developed into a distinct religion.
Roman roads, a common administration and Constantine's 313 toleration enabled Christianity's spread and its eventual official acceptance.
Pax Romana's secure roads and sea routes eased missionary travel, helping early Christian communities spread across the empire.
Early Christian communities produced the gospels and epistles that were later canonized as the New Testament.
Disputes over the nature of Christ within the church produced Arianism, a major doctrinal controversy.
Christians' refusal to honor Roman gods and their growing numbers prompted Diocletian's persecution of Christians.
India's independence in 1947 led to the 1949 Indo-Bhutanese treaty, which placed Bhutan's external relations under Indian guidance.
Wartime demands for codebreaking and ballistics calculation drove governments to build the first electronic computers, such as Colossus and ENIAC.
Cold War military funding for defense research accelerated computer development in the United States and Soviet Union.
Networked computers developed for research laid the technical basis on which Tim Berners-Lee built the World Wide Web in 1989.
Miniaturized, affordable computing hardware and software made possible the personal computers marketed from the late 1950s onward.
Computer networks developed on time-sharing systems allowed the first electronic mail messages to be sent between users in 1971.
The Bolshevik seizure of power in the October Revolution created the Soviet state, which was formally proclaimed in 1922.
Stalin's forced collectivization and grain requisitions in Soviet Ukraine caused the 1932-1933 Holodomor famine.
Soviet diplomacy produced the 1939 Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact with Nazi Germany, dividing Eastern Europe into spheres of influence.
Stalin's consolidation of power led to the Great Purge of 1936-1938, which executed or imprisoned much of the Communist leadership.
World War II weakened British imperial power and fuelled Caribbean demands for self-government, leading to Jamaican independence in 1962.
Muhammad's oral revelations were memorized and recorded by his followers, forming the basis of the Quranic text.
Caliph Uthman ordered the copying of a single standard text of the Quran, which became the authoritative codex.
Abu Bakr ordered the first collection of Muhammad's revelations into written form after the battle of Yamama.
English colonial expansion sent settlers to Barbados in the 1620s, establishing a plantation colony under the English crown.
Christopher Columbus sighted and named Grenada on his third voyage in 1498, bringing the island into Spanish colonial claims.
Spanish colonization of the Americas, launched after Columbus's voyages, brought Grenada into Spanish imperial claims in the Caribbean.
The four-stroke internal combustion engine supplied the power unit that made practical self-propelled road vehicles possible.
Cheap steel production from the Bessemer process gave automobile makers strong, light chassis and engine materials.
The Yalta Conference divided postwar Europe into Soviet and Western spheres, setting the division that NATO later institutionalized.
Migration Period invasions drove refugees from the Veneto mainland into the Venetian lagoon, where they founded settlements.
The decline of Roman authority in northern Italy left the lagoon communities to govern themselves.
Electrical science, including the electric battery and telegraph current, provided the principles on which Bell's 1876 telephone transmitted speech.
Telephony's wireless transmission principles and switching networks were developed into the cellular mobile phones deployed from the 1970s.
Volta's 1800 electric battery gave researchers a steady current source, enabling the experiments that established electricity as a field.
Faraday's electromagnetic induction research of the early 1830s, building on electrical experiments, led to the first transformers.
Faraday's 1821 electromagnetic rotation experiments grew into the electric motors demonstrated in the 1830s.
Electromagnetic theory and spark-gap experiments gave Marconi and others the means to transmit radio signals in 1894-1901.
Mongol conquests destroyed the Seljuk sultanate and fragmented Anatolia into beyliks, letting Osman's successors expand.
The Crusades weakened Byzantine power in the eastern Mediterranean, creating space for Turkish principalities to expand.
Ottoman forces under Murad II defeated the Hungarian-led Crusade at Varna in 1444, consolidating Ottoman control of the Balkans.
Ottoman control of Levantine and Egyptian trade routes raised costs for Europeans, pushing Portugal to seek sea routes to Asia.
Octavian's victory at Actium in 31 BC gave him sole command of Rome's armies, ending the Republic and founding the Principate.
Julius Caesar's dictatorship and the civil wars after his assassination broke the Republic's institutions and paved the way for imperial rule.
Rome's victories over Carthage in the Punic Wars gave it control of the western Mediterranean and the resources to expand into an empire.
Roman imperial expansion under Claudius invaded Britain in 43 CE, bringing the southern island into the empire.
Early Christian communities organized around bishops and presbyters, and this structure developed into the institutional Catholic Church.
Roman administrative structure and the prestige of the Roman bishopric in Rome gave the early church its hierarchy and central see.
The deposition of the last Western emperor in 476 ended unified imperial rule in the West, leaving Germanic kingdoms to shape medieval Europe.
Germanic and Hunnic migrations across the Roman frontiers reshaped the political map, founding the early medieval kingdoms.
Reformation pamphlet wars created a mass demand for printed polemic, encouraging the early periodical press.
Newspapers and periodicals spread Enlightenment ideas to a wide literate public, shaping eighteenth-century debate.
Cheap steel tubing and improved steel production made lightweight bicycle frames practical in the 1880s.
Bicycle engineering, including chain drive and wire-spoked wheels, taught the Wright brothers the balance and control principles they applied to their aircraft.
Christian belief in Peter as the first bishop of Rome gave the Roman see a special primacy that developed into the papal office.
The Roman bishop's central position in the capital of the Roman Empire helped establish the see's prestige among western churches.
Jesus's teaching and crucifixion were the subject of the early Gospels, which were written down and became the core of the New Testament.
Automobile engine development gave aviation pioneers lightweight internal combustion engines suited to powering early aircraft.
The French Revolution proclaimed popular sovereignty in the name of the nation, and Napoleon's conquests carried national identity across Europe.
Romantic writers and historians celebrated folk language, history and national culture, giving nationalist movements their emotional vocabulary.
The partitions of Poland erased the Polish state, and the loss of sovereignty fuelled a Polish national movement seeking independence.
Hertz's 1886-1888 experiments demonstrated electromagnetic waves, which Marconi and others then adapted into radio signalling.
The Black Death's mass mortality disrupted feudal labor and wealth, loosening traditional structures that Italian city-states then exploited for new patronage and learning.
Dante's vernacular Divine Comedy and classical learning set the literary models that Italian humanists later extended.
Erasmus and other humanists returned to Greek and Latin sources, providing the scholarly tools Luther used to challenge Church doctrine.
Late Renaissance humanists in Florence revived Greek drama ideals, leading the Camerata to create opera around 1600.
The Soviet launch of Sputnik in 1957 triggered the US space race, and Congress created NASA in 1958 in response.
The collapse of Austria-Hungary at the end of World War I let Serbs, Croats and Slovenes proclaim a common South Slav state in 1918.
The Balkan Wars enlarged Serbia and encouraged South Slav unification projects that culminated in the Yugoslav state.
The postwar settlement at Versailles and its partner treaties recognized the Yugoslav kingdom and fixed its borders.
Martin Luther's 1517 Ninety-five Theses and his later refusal to recant launched the Protestant break with Rome.
Gutenberg-style printing let Luther's pamphlets and vernacular Bibles circulate widely, spreading reformed doctrine across Europe.
Adolf Hitler, as NSDAP leader and then chancellor in 1933, dismantled democratic institutions and directed the Nazi state.
The Versailles settlement's territorial losses and reparations fuelled German resentment that the Nazis exploited.
The Great Depression's mass unemployment collapsed support for the Weimar parties and carried the NSDAP to power in 1933.
The weaknesses of the Weimar constitution, including emergency decree powers, allowed Hitler to become chancellor and then end the republic.
Hitler's invasion of Poland in September 1939 triggered Britain and France's declarations of war, starting World War II.
The Nazi regime's racial policies and state-run mass murder produced the Holocaust, killing six million European Jews.
German military defeat of France in 1940 and the armistice terms established the Vichy regime under German occupation.
The East Frankish kingdom, which Otto I ruled, became the core of the empire when he was crowned emperor in 962.
Charlemagne's imperial coronation in 800 gave the later German kings a claim to Carolingian imperial title and legitimacy.
Otto I's decisive defeat of the Magyars at Lechfeld in 955 enhanced his authority, leading to his imperial coronation in 962.
The Treaty of Verdun divided the Carolingian realm, creating the East Frankish kingdom from which the empire later grew.
Advances in computing and microelectronics supplied the processors and software that made handheld cellular phones practical.
Satellite communication research supported the wide-area radio links and network concepts used by early cellular systems.
